elements.problem: The page's criterion is the duration of a pain episode (lasts >= 10 minutes). The language has no episode-duration construct, so the builder used the onset time of the Chest pain finding: 'onset at least 10 minutes ago' in the ACS rule and 'onset within the last 10 minutes' in the stable angina rule. The comparator directions follow the briefing's onset convention, but the semantics are wrong in practice: almost every patient presents more than 10 minutes after the pain began, so the ACS disjunct is nearly always true (making the other four characteristics and the stable-angina exclusion irrelevant) and the stable angina rule, which requires onset within the last 10 minutes, is nearly unreachable. Either this item should be left out with a not_representable note, or the stable angina rule at least should not require it.

rule_level_problems.rule: Diagnose probable stable angina in chest pain
rule_level_problems.problem: Requires (<= (onset Chest pain) (time_ago 10 minutes)), i.e. the pain began within the last 10 minutes. Onset is not episode duration; patients almost never present inside 10 minutes of onset, so the stable angina rule is effectively unreachable and the matching (>= onset 10 minutes) disjunct makes the ACS rule fire for nearly every chest-pain presentation on the ECG-abnormal or no-positional path, regardless of the other four characteristics or known stable angina. The 'Lasts >= 10 minutes' item should be dropped as not representable (or at least removed from the stable angina rule) rather than approximated with onset.

rule_level_problems.rule: Diagnose probable acute coronary syndrome in chest pain / Diagnose probable stable angina in chest pain / Check chest pain character for acute coronary syndrome
rule_level_problems.problem: Two of the five 'Is chest pain/discomfort any of' items are absent from the check_for list and from both diagnosis rules: 'Not relieved by rest or sublingual nitrates' and 'Occurs more often than usual'; 'with minimal effort' is also lost. Because the stable angina rule is the negation of the same list, a known stable-angina patient with either missing feature is diagnosed stable angina where the page says ACS. No remaining-questions note is visible to me, and SNOMED offers Chest pain + (snomed_concept "Frequent" "qualifier value") or "Increased" for the frequency item, and the "Relieved by" attribute / "Relieved" qualifier for the nitrate item.

rule_level_problems.rule: Diagnose probable tension pneumothorax in chest pain
rule_level_problems.problem: The page's comma list ('sudden breathlessness, more resonant/decreased breath sounds/pain on one side, deviated trachea') is encoded as all-of: sudden dyspnoea AND a unilateral sign AND tracheal deviation. Tracheal deviation is a late sign; if the page means any-of, or sudden breathlessness plus any one sign, the rule under-fires. The reading is defensible but should be flagged for the clinician. 'Pain on one side' is encoded as plain Left/Right sided chest pain, which the red-box 'New left sided chest pain' record will also satisfy; acceptable.

rule_level_problems.rule: Diagnose probable acute coronary syndrome in chest pain / Diagnose probable stable angina in chest pain / Diagnose probable pneumonia in chest pain
rule_level_problems.problem: The probable rules use (clinical_finding (snomed_concept "Chest pain" "finding")) and (>= (measurement "Body temperature") 38) as evidence without any check_for for them in this file. Chest pain is a recorded warning sign and temperature a routine vital, so this is presumably allowed by the test, but I cannot confirm it from the inputs allowed here. Likewise the pulse measurement uses "Pulse, function" where SNOMED also has "Heart rate"; it must match the concept VHA records for the pulse vital.

Footnote 5's 'shock likely' (SBP < 80, pulse >= 100, RR > 30, confusion/restlessness, weakness) has no probable Shock rule. It gates a management step, so this is a judgment call, but the briefing's rule is every 'X likely' becomes a probable diagnosis.

summary: The 'Lasts >= 10 minutes' criterion is approximated with the onset time of the Chest pain finding, which makes the ACS rule fire for almost any chest pain on the ECG-abnormal or non-positional path and makes the stable angina rule (onset within the last 10 minutes) practically unreachable. Two of the five ACS character items ('Not relieved by rest or sublingual nitrates', 'Occurs more often than usual') and 'with minimal effort' are not encoded at all, so a known stable-angina patient with those features is labelled stable angina where the page says ACS. The red-box priority rule, the ECG task, the positional question, the pneumonia rule and the tension pneumothorax rule are otherwise complete and use existing SNOMED concepts; the pneumothorax rule's all-of reading of the page's comma list should be confirmed with a clinician.
